claim: RAS family proteins are amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers.
source: The RAS family of proteins is amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers and has so far eluded drug therapy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Downward, 2003; Prior et al., 2012) and reference to the COSMIC database.

claim: RAS has so far eluded drug therapy.
source: The RAS family of proteins is amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers and has so far eluded drug therapy.
evidence: This is supported by citations and the statement that there are still no RAS-targeted drugs currently available in the clinic.

claim: BRET-based RAS biosensors enable monitoring of RAS-effector interaction inhibition in living cells.
source: Here, we have developed a robust set of bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based RAS biosensors that enable monitoring of RAS-effector interaction inhibition in living cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing BRET signal changes in transfected cells with various RAS-effector combinations.

claim: The RAS biosensors include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS with various mutations that mirror those found in human cancers.
source: These include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS and a variety of different mutations that mirror those found in human cancers with the major RAS effectors such as CRAF, PI3K and RALGDS.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing biosensors for multiple RAS isoforms and mutants.

claim: A RAS-binding compound (3344) is a potent pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor in cells.
source: We highlighted the utility of these RAS biosensors by showing a RAS-binding compound is a potent pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor in cells.
evidence: This is supported by BRET assay data showing dose-dependent inhibition across multiple RAS-effector pairs and X-ray crystallography showing binding.

claim: Mutation in RAS proteins can be found in approximately 30% of all human tumors.
source: Mutation in RAS proteins can be found in approximately 30% of all human tumors (Downward, 2003; Prior et al., 2012) (http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and reference to the COSMIC database.

claim: There are still no RAS-targeted drugs currently available in the clinic.
source: However, there are still no RAS-targeted drugs currently available in the clinic even though such molecules could prove widely efficacious in many human cancers as front-line drugs for therapy.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the current state of RAS drug development.

claim: Pancreatic cancer contains a high proportion of KRAS mutations.
source: Some forms of cancer, like pancreatic cancer, present late and are difficult therefore to treat (Kleeff et al., 2016) but these contain a high proportion of KRAS mutations and are thus potentially susceptible to RAS-binding drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAS has been regarded as undruggable partly because attempts to interfere with the protein have not been efficacious.
source: RAS has been regarded as undruggable partly because so far attempts to interfere with the protein have not been efficacious (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAS is a membrane-bound small GTPase switching between an inactive GDP-bound state and an active GTP-bound state.
source: RAS is a membrane-bound small GTPase switching between an inactive GDP-bound state and an active GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAS protein biochemistry.

claim: RAS signaling to the cell nucleus occurs after interaction of RAS-GTP with its effectors to trigger the activation of downstream signaling pathways.
source: RAS signaling to the cell nucleus occurs after interaction of RAS-GTP with its effectors to trigger the activation of downstream signaling pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RAS signaling mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: RAS activation promotes cell survival and cell proliferation via gene modulation.
source: This activation thereby promotes cell survival and cell proliferation (Wennerberg et al., 2005) via gene modulation
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Farnesylation inhibitors have limited success due to side effects.
source: methods such as implementing farnesylation inhibitors have limited success due to side effects (Berndt et al., 2011; James et al., 1995; Whyte et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Intracellular antibodies that block effector interaction sites of RAS-GTP can prevent tumor growth in xenograft models and tumor initiation in a transgenic mouse model.
source: This PPI inhibition can prevent tumor growth in xenograft models and tumor initiation in a transgenic mouse model (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2010; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published experimental studies.

claim: RAS was regarded as a protein without any pockets suitable for small molecule interactions for many years.
source: Moreover, for many years, RAS was regarded as a protein without any pockets suitable for small molecule interactions (McCormick, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Recent studies have described compounds that are able to bind RAS-associated pockets.
source: but recent studies have described compounds that are able to bind RAS-associated pockets (Gentile et al., 2017; Lito et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2012; Ostrem et al., 2013; Patricelli et al., 2016; Shima et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2012; Waldmann et al., 2004; Welsch et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Most current RAS inhibitors have been selected and identified through in vitro techniques.
source: Most of the current RAS inhibitors have been selected and identified through in vitro techniques (Ostrem et al., 2013; Trinh et al., 2016; Upadhyaya et al., 2015; Welsch et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A robust cell-based assay is a mandatory step in any drug discovery programme.
source: Indeed, a robust cell-based assay is a mandatory step in any drug discovery programme, as it provides insights into the behavior of compounds in physiological conditions, including cell permeability, stability and potency in the cellular complexity of a whole cell.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of drug discovery practices.

claim: RLuc8 was fused to the amino termini of full-length RAS family proteins and GFP2 fused to the C-termini of the effectors or iDAbs.
source: Hence, RLuc8 was fused to the amino termini of full-length RAS family proteins and the GFP2 (Ramsay et al., 2002) fused to the C-termini of the effectors (RALGDS, CRAF, PI3K) or of the iDAbs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the biosensor constructs.

claim: A higher BRET signal was observed with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct and a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule.
source: For our study, we observed a higher BRET signal with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct, a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule and a (GGGS)2 linker between iDAb RAS-GFP2 construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: If an interaction occurs between RAS and a partner-GFP2 fusion, bringing the RLuc8 and GFP2 within 100 Å, an energy transfer occurs from the RLuc8-RAS donor to the GFP2 acceptor and a BRET2 signal is achieved.
source: If an interaction occurs between RAS and a partner-GFP2 fusion, bringing the RLuc8 and GFP2 within 100 Å, an energy transfer occurs from the RLuc8-RAS donor to the GFP2 acceptor and a BRET2 signal is achieved (Figure 1A, middle panel).
evidence: This describes the principle of BRET2 technology, which is established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: All of the effector domains were found to interact specifically with KRASG12D since the BRET signal reached a donor saturation level.
source: All of the effector domains were found to interact specifically with KRASG12D since the BRET signal reached a donor saturation level (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All the transfected plasmids expressed the proteins at equivalent levels as indicated by western blot analysis.
source: Further, all the transfected plasmids expressed the proteins at equivalent levels as indicated by western blot analysis (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The dominant negative mutant KRASS17N does not interact with the effectors.
source: To further characterize this BRET2 system, we used the dominant negative mutant KRASS17N, which does not interact with the effectors (Cool et al., 1999; Nassar et al., 2010; van den Berghe et al., 1997), as a donor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: The BRET signal increased linearly with the concentration of acceptor for KRASS17N with all the RAS binding domains, which is typical of non-specific interactions.
source: We found that the BRET signal increased linearly with the concentration of acceptor for all the RAS binding domains. This result is typical of non-specific interactions (Mercier et al., 2002), confirming the S17N mutant does not interact with the effectors and supports the sensitivity of this system (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation to published literature on BRET interpretation.

claim: iDAb RAS interacts with mutant KRAS on the switch regions.
source: We initially characterized the biosensor pairs with the iDAb RAS that is known to interact with mutant KRAS on the switch regions (Tanaka et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Dematured iDAb RAS (iDAbdm RAS) has reduced affinity towards RAS-GTP from 6.2 nM to ~1 μM affinity.
source: Introduction of mutations in the three CDRs of the iDAb RAS to generate a dematured iDAb RAS (iDAbdm RAS), was shown to reduce its affinity towards RAS-GTP from 6.2 nM to ~1 μM affinity (Assi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: iDAbdm RAS significantly increased the BRET50 and significantly reduced the BRETmax compared to iDAb RAS.
source: Indeed, it significantly increased the BRET50 (an approximation of the relative affinity of the acceptor fusion for the donor fusion proteins, corresponding to the acceptor/donor ratio necessary to reach 50% of the BRETmax) and significantly reduced the BRETmax (an approximation for the total number of complex RAS/iDAb and the distance between the donor and the acceptor within the dimer), which together are consistent with a decreased affinity of this mutant iDAb toward RAS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: iDAb RAS, but not the control, drastically decreased the BRET ratio of all the KRASG12D-effector interactions tested.
source: This competition showed that iDAb RAS, but not the control, drastically decreased the BRET ratio of all the interactions tested (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Compound 3344 binds to KRASG12V with an affinity of 126 nM using 1H CPMG NMR.
source: We have identified compounds that bind to KRAS using in vitro screening and one compound 3344 (chemical structure and 1-D NMR characterization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C) binds to KRASG12V with an affinity of 126 nM using 1H Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) NMR (Baldwin and Kay, 2009) (data are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by NMR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In vitro competition studies show the anti-RAS scFv inhibits 3344 binding to KRAS.
source: In vitro competition studies of 3344 binding to KRASG12V in waterLOGSY NMR show the anti-RAS scFv inhibits 3344 binding to KRAS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by waterLOGSY NMR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Compound 3344 shows a dose response reduction in BRET signal for assays with KRASG12D and various effectors (PI3Kα RBD, PI3Kγ RBD, CRAF RBD, RALGDS RA).
source: We observed a dose response reduction in BRET signal for the assays with compound 3344 but not with the Abd-2 indicating that only 3344 interferes with the RAS-effector PPI (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental BRET data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Abd-2 does not interfere with the RAS-effector PPI.
source: We observed a dose response reduction in BRET signal for the assays with compound 3344 but not with the Abd-2 indicating that only 3344 interferes with the RAS-effector PPI (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental BRET data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 3344 only interferes, in a dose response, with KRASG12D/iDAbdm RAS-induced BRET without affecting the expression of the biosensors.
source: Abd-2 has no effect on any of these assays while 3344 only interferes, in a dose response, with KRASG12D/iDAbdm RAS-induced BRET without affecting the expression of the biosensors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3I and 3J.

claim: The CRAFS257L mutation increases ERK phosphorylation.
source: To reduce this limitation, we developed an optimized RAS biosensor of the full-length CRAFS257L mutant (herein named CRAFFL) since the S257L mutation increases ERK phosphorylation (Razzaque et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CRAFFL interacts with KRASG12D but not with KRASS17N.
source: and because we found that CRAFFL interacts with KRASG12D but not with KRASS17N (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: iDAb RAS impedes the BRET2 signal due to the binding of CRAFFL with KRASG12D in a dose response mode, whereas the iDAb control had no effect.
source: We performed a competition assay with the iDAb RAS confirming that it impedes the BRET2 signal due to the binding of CRAFFL with KRASG12D, in a dose response mode, whereas the iDAb control had no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: iDAb RAS inhibition significantly decreased the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases.
source: In addition, iDAb RAS inhibition significantly decreased the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases (Figure 2B shows western blot data, quantitated in Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2C.

claim: Compound 3344 significantly decreases BRET signal with KRASG12D/CRAFFL biosensor in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We compared the effect of Abd-2 and 3344 on the BRET pair and found a significant decrease in BRET signal with 3344 that occurred in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Compound 3344 significantly inhibited MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation whilst Abd-2 did not.
source: Western blots using anti-pMEK and anti-pERK showed that 3344 also significantly inhibited MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation whilst Abd-2 did not (Figure 2E, quantified in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E and quantified in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: Compound 3344 shows a dose response effect on KRASG12A, KRASG12C, KRASG12V and KRASG12R interaction with CRAFFL but Abd-2 does not.
source: Analysis of the BRET2 signals from interaction of KRASG12A, KRASG12C, KRASG12V and KRASG12R with CRAFFL showed a dose response effect of compound 3344 but not Abd-2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: EGF treatment brings KRASWT and CRAFFL fusion proteins in a closer proximity and enhances the number of KRASWT/CRAFFL dimers because the BRETmax value increases from 4.02 to 10.01.
source: EGF treatment brings KRASWT and CRAFFL fusion proteins in a closer proximity and enhances the number of KRASWT/CRAFFL dimers because the BRETmax value increases from 4.02 to 10.01 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A dose response inhibition of the BRET2 signal was observed with iDAb RAS, but not iDAb control, for KRASWT/CRAFFL interaction.
source: A dose response inhibition of the BRET2 signal was observed with iDAb RAS, but not iDAb control (Figure 3A), which correlated with the reduction of pMEK1/2 and pERK1/2 detected by western blots (Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and 3C.

claim: Compound 3344 inhibits KRASWT/CRAFFL interaction in a dose-response manner.
source: Compound 3344 inhibits this interaction in a dose-response manner (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and prevents the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases (Figure 3E, quantified in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, 3E, 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, 1E, 1F.

claim: Co-expression of the p85α regulatory subunit with PI3KαFL-GFP2 was required to obtain detectable, specific and optimized BRET signal from interaction of KRASG12D and PI3KαFL.
source: In this case, we required a tripartite system as we observed that co-expression of the p85α regulatory subunit with PI3KαFL-GFP2 was required to obtain detectable, specific and optimized BRET signal from interaction of KRASG12D and PI3KαFL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: KRASS17N mutant showed no specific interaction with PI3KαFL.
source: KRASS17N mutant showed no specific interaction with PI3KαFL further confirming the accuracy of this biosensor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: iDAb RAS impaired KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the iDAb control did not.
source: We validated the BRET biosensor by showing that the iDAb RAS impaired that interaction in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the iDAb control did not (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: iDAb RAS caused a dose response reduction of phosphorylation of the downstream biomarker AKT at Ser473.
source: and there was also a dose response reduction of phosphorylation of the downstream biomarker AKT at Ser473 (Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4C.

claim: Compound 3344 interferes with the KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction.
source: Implementing the same biosensor assay treated with the compound 3344 for 3 or 20 hr, we confirmed this compound interferes with the KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Compound 3344 causes dose response reduction of BRET signal with KRASG12D/PI3KαFL but Abd-2 does not.
source: When increasing doses of either Abd-2 or 3344 were used in the BRET-transfected cells, we observed dose response reduction of BRET signal with 3344 but not Abd-2 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Compound 3344 causes a reduction in the downstream biomarker AKT Ser473 phosphorylation.
source: Associated with this inhibition, was a reduction in the downstream biomarker AKT Ser473 phosphorylation (Figure 4E, quantified in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E and quantified in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: KRAS, NRAS and HRAS family members have an almost identical amino-acid domain (G domain) from residues 1–166 but a C-terminal hypervariable domain.
source: The KRAS, NRAS and HRAS family members are conserved proteins that have an almost identical amino-acid domain (G domain) from residues 1–166 but a C-terminal hypervariable domain (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RLuc8-NRASQ61H and RLuc8-HRASG12V proteins interact and reach plateau BRET signals with GFP2-CRAFFL.
source: Titration of the RAS donor and CRAFFL acceptor proteins show that the RLuc8-NRASQ61H and RLuc8-HRASG12V proteins interact and reach plateau BRET signals with GFP2-CRAFFL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The BRET2 signal from NRASQ61H/CRAFFL and HRASG12V/CRAFFL is diminished by increasing levels of the iDAb RAS but not the iDAb control.
source: Furthermore, the BRET2 signal is diminished by increasing levels of the iDAb RAS but not the iDAb control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Abd-2 compound does not interfere with the BRET signal in any of the NRAS and HRAS BRET assays using either effector RBDs or full-length CRAF.
source: While the low-affinity Abd-2 compound does not interfere with the BRET signal in any of the NRAS and HRAS BRET assays using either effector RBDs (Figure 5A,B) or full-length CRAF (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: Compound 3344 disturbs the BRET2 signal in a dose-response manner in all NRAS and HRAS interactions with effectors.
source: the compound 3344 disturbs the BRET2 signal in a dose-response manner in all these RAS interactions (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Compound 3344 binds to KRAS in a previously identified pocket close to the switch regions where the effectors interact with RAS.
source: Figure 6A shows that 3344 binds to KRAS in a previously identified pocket (Maurer et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012) close to the switch regions where the effectors interact with RAS (Table 1 has the refinement statistics for the X-ray data).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 6A and citations to published literature.

claim: Parts of 3344 would overlap with the bound effector structures, suggesting that the competition effect of 3344 can be explained by straightforward steric hindrance.
source: The superimposition of the structures of three RAS-effector protein complexes with the structure of KRAS-3344 complex shows that parts of 3344 would overlap with the bound effector structures, suggesting that the competition effect of 3344 can be explained by straightforward steric hindrance (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Compound 3344 decreases EGF-induced pAKT and pERK1/2 abundance in DLD-1 and H358 cells with an observed IC50 of ~5–10 μM without any change in the total levels of AKT or ERK1/2.
source: 3344 decreases EGF-induced pAKT and pERK1/2 abundance in both cell types with an observed IC50 of ~5–10 μM without any change in the total levels of AKT or ERK1/2.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: DLD-1 cells express KRASG13D.
source: We further confirmed that 3344 could interfere with the endogenous RAS-effector PPI in two human cancer cell lines (viz. colorectal adenocarcinoma DLD-1 cells expressing KRASG13D
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: H358 cells express KRASG12C.
source: and non-small cell lung carcinoma H358 cells expressing KRASG12C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: BRET-based biosensors have been successfully used to discover and characterize small molecules inhibitors.
source: BRET-based biosensors have been successfully used to discover and characterize small molecules inhibitors (Beautrait et al., 2017; Corbel et al., 2011; Lavoie et al., 2013; Mazars and Fåhraeus, 2010; Robinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The RAS biosensors provide a direct and quantitative measurement of the PPI interference with inhibitors.
source: It provides a direct and quantitative measurement of the PPI interference with inhibitors (i.e. small molecules or macrodrugs), which could allow the comparison of different compounds (e.g. for structure-activity-relationship studies) or macrodrugs and therefore the selection of more potent inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated capabilities of the BRET assay system.

claim: Compound 3344 prevents endogenous RAS-dependent signaling in two different human tumor cell lines at a lower concentration (IC50 around 5 μM) than in the BRET assay with observed IC50 around 20 μM.
source: Nonetheless, 3344 prevents endogenous RAS-dependent signaling in two different human tumor cell lines at a lower concentration (IC50 around 5 μM) (Figure 6C,D) than in the BRET assay with observed IC50 around 20 μM.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 6C,D with BRET assay data.

claim: The difference in IC50 between BRET assay and endogenous assay probably reflects the expression levels of the target proteins in the two assays.
source: This difference probably reflects the expression levels of the target proteins in the two assays, where the BRET2 assay relies on transient transfection.
evidence: This is based on logical inference from the experimental design.

claim: The overexpression in HEK293T cells probably produces higher amount of mutant RAS/effector proteins than the endogenous counterparts in cancer cells.
source: Indeed, the overexpression in HEK293T cells probably produces higher amount of mutant RAS/effector proteins than the endogenous counterparts in cancer cells.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about transient transfection versus endogenous expression.

claim: Studies suggested that isoform and residue- or codon-specific RAS mutants show differences in their ability to engage effectors and signaling properties.
source: Indeed, studies suggested that isoform and residue- or codon-specific RAS mutants show differences in their ability to engage effectors and signaling properties (Hunter et al., 2015; Nakhaeizadeh et al., 2016; Yan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RAS biosensors could be a methodology to decipher RAS isoform/mutant properties in cells.
source: Accordingly, RAS biosensors could also be a methodology to decipher RAS isoform/mutant properties in cells.
evidence: This is based on inference from the capabilities of the biosensor system.

claim: The BRET2 biosensor system could be used for direct screens of PPI inhibitors with libraries of compounds.
source: The BRET2 biosensor system could also be used for direct screens of PPI inhibitors with libraries of compounds.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential applications of the biosensor system.

claim: Initial compounds from a library are not expected to have high affinity for their target.
source: However, because initial compounds from a library are not expected to have high affinity for their target, relatively weak interactions between donor and acceptors should be involved in the generation of BRET2 signal.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of drug discovery practices.

claim: Reduction of affinity (dematuration) of an intracellular domain antibody from a tool initially used for target validation can be achieved to make a screening tool.
source: This provides a further use of intracellular domain antibodies where reduction of affinity (dematuration) from a tool initially used for target validation, can be achieved to make a screening tool.
evidence: This is based on inference from the demonstrated use of iDAbdm RAS in the study.

claim: The method is an approach that is transferable to other PPI situations required for drug development programmes in cancer or any other clinical indication.
source: Thus, the method is an approach that is transferable to other PPI situations required for drug development programmes in cancer or any other clinical indication.
evidence: This is based on inference about the general applicability of the BRET biosensor approach.
